seo_title: Insurance Appraisal Timeline Explained: Stage by Stage
meta_description: Insurance appraisal timeline explained: the 10 stages from claim to award, how long Texas appraisals take, what causes delays and how to stay on track.
h1: Insurance Appraisal Timeline Explained: What to Expect at Each Stage
secondary_keywords: how long does insurance appraisal take
excerpt: Most Texas residential appraisals take about one to three months. See the insurance appraisal timeline explained stage by stage, plus what causes delays and how to avoid them.
key_takeaways: Most residential appraisals take about one to three months after appraisers are named.
Many policies require appraisers named within 20 days of the demand.
Umpire disputes and missing documentation are the biggest sources of delay.
Choosing your appraiser early and organizing evidence speeds up the process.
body_html:
The insurance appraisal timeline, explained simply: most residential appraisals in Texas take about one to three months from the written demand to a signed award. Each side names an appraiser, often within 20 days, the appraisers pick an umpire, inspect, exchange estimates and negotiate. Complex or commercial claims can take several months longer.

When a claim dispute drags on, homeowners want to know one thing: how long will this take? Appraisal is usually much faster than a lawsuit, but it is not instant. Knowing each stage, what normally happens in it, and what causes delays helps you plan repairs, keep the process moving and avoid surprises.

What is insurance appraisal?

Appraisal is a dispute resolution process written into most Texas homeowners and commercial property policies. It applies when you and your insurer agree there is covered damage but disagree on the amount of loss. Each side hires an appraiser, an umpire decides anything the appraisers cannot agree on, and an award signed by two of the three sets the amount. For a full introduction, see what an insurance appraisal is.

Appraisal decides the amount of loss, not coverage. Under State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (Tex. 2009), appraisers may consider whether damage was caused by the storm, but questions about whether the policy covers the loss stay outside appraisal.

The insurance appraisal timeline at a glance

StageWhat happensTypical duration
1. Claim filedLoss reported, claim acknowledgedDays; Texas carriers generally must acknowledge within 15 days
2. Inspection and estimateAdjuster inspects and issues estimateWeeks, longer after major storms
3. Pre-appraisal negotiationSupplements, reinspections, rebuttalsWeeks to months
4. Appraisal demandWritten demand under the appraisal clauseOne day to send
5. Appraisers namedEach side selects an appraiserOften within 20 days under many policies
6. Umpire selectedAppraisers agree, or a court appointsOften about 15 days; longer if a court is needed
7. Joint inspectionAppraisers inspect the property1 to 3 weeks to schedule
8. Estimates and negotiationLine-item estimates exchanged and discussed2 to 6 weeks
9. Umpire reviewOnly if appraisers disagree2 to 6 weeks
10. Award and paymentAward signed; carrier paysAward in days; payment per policy and Texas law

Durations are general ranges, not promises. Your policy's appraisal clause controls the specific deadlines that apply to you.

Stages one to four: from claim to appraisal demand

Stage one: filing the claim

The clock starts when you report the loss. Under Texas Insurance Code Chapter 542, insurers generally must acknowledge the claim within 15 days, then accept or reject it within 15 business days after receiving the information they requested, with extensions up to 45 days in some situations. Our Texas claim deadline calculator helps track these dates.

Stage two: inspection and estimate

The carrier inspects and issues an estimate. After large Texas hail or hurricane events, this step can take weeks because adjusters are stretched thin.

Stage three: negotiation before appraisal

Before invoking appraisal, most policyholders submit supplements, request reinspections, and send written rebuttals with photos and estimates. This stage often resolves smaller disputes without appraisal at all.

Stage four: the formal appraisal demand

When negotiation stalls, either party can send a written appraisal demand. It should identify the claim, the disputed amount, and, ideally, your selected appraiser. See what happens after invoking the appraisal clause in Texas.

Stages five to ten: inside the appraisal process

Stage five: selecting appraisers

Many policies require each side to name a competent and disinterested appraiser within a set period after the demand, commonly 20 days. Choosing your appraiser before sending the demand saves time.

Stage six: selecting the umpire

The two appraisers try to agree on an umpire. Many policy forms give them about 15 days; if they cannot agree, either side can ask a court to appoint one, which adds time. Learn more in how insurance umpires are chosen in Texas.

Stage seven: joint property inspection

The appraisers inspect the property, often together. They walk the roof, review interior damage and may take measurements or test cuts. Good access and organized documentation make this step go faster.

Stage eight: estimates and negotiation

Each appraiser prepares or reviews a line-item estimate. They compare them, resolve what they can and narrow the disputed items. Many appraisals end here with an agreed award.

Stage nine: umpire review

If items remain disputed, the appraisers submit them to the umpire with supporting evidence. The umpire may review documents, ask questions or inspect the property. The umpire is neutral and does not represent either side.

Stage ten: the appraisal award

An award signed by any two of the three panel members sets the amount of loss. The carrier then pays according to the policy, generally less prior payments, the deductible and any non-recoverable depreciation.

How long does insurance appraisal usually take?

  • Simple claims (single roof, clear documentation): often about 30 to 60 days after appraisers are named.
  • Moderate claims (roof plus interior, some scope disputes): often about 60 to 90 days.
  • Complex claims (large homes, commercial buildings, multiple structures, engineering issues): several months or more.

These ranges reflect common experience, not promises. For more detail, see how long an insurance appraisal takes.

What commonly delays insurance appraisal?

  • Slow communication: unanswered emails and slow document exchanges add weeks.
  • Incomplete documentation: missing photos, estimates or invoices stall negotiation.
  • Umpire disputes: if appraisers cannot agree on an umpire, a court appointment adds time.
  • Hidden damage discoveries: new damage found during the process may require more inspection.
  • Scope disagreements: repair vs. replace, matching and causation questions take longer to resolve.
  • Storm season backlogs: after major Texas weather events, appraisers, umpires and contractors are busy.
Tip: Choose your appraiser before you send the demand, and have your documentation organized from day one. Those two steps remove the most common early delays.

Texas storm seasons and the appraisal calendar

In Texas, timing often depends on the weather calendar. Spring hail season in North and Central Texas and hurricane season along the Gulf Coast can produce thousands of claims at once. When many appraisals start around the same time, experienced umpires book up, contractors are hard to schedule for joint inspections, and carriers' appraisers juggle large caseloads. If your claim falls in one of these periods, build in extra time and keep pressing gently, in writing, to maintain momentum. Homeowners in places like Dallas, Fort Worth and Houston see this effect most after major events.

Can insurance appraisal be expedited?

You cannot force the other side to move faster, but you can remove the delays you control. The fastest appraisals usually share a few traits:

  • The policyholder's appraiser is named in the demand letter itself.
  • A complete documentation package, including photos, measurements and a line-item estimate, is ready before the first inspection.
  • The appraisers propose umpire candidates immediately rather than waiting until the deadline.
  • Inspection dates are offered promptly, with roof and interior access arranged.
  • Disputes are narrowed to specific line items early, so the umpire, if needed, reviews only a short list.

As an illustrative example, a straightforward hail roof dispute where both appraisers are named within a week, agree on an umpire quickly and inspect together in the second week can often reach an agreed award within about a month. The same claim can stretch to three months or more if documents trickle in and the umpire has to be appointed by a court.

What homeowners should do during the appraisal timeline

  1. Stay organized: keep the policy, estimates, photos and correspondence in one place.
  2. Respond quickly to requests from your appraiser and to inspection scheduling.
  3. Document everything, especially if temporary repairs are needed. Our claim documentation checklist helps.
  4. Understand your policy, including the appraisal clause, deductibles and depreciation terms.
  5. Keep contractors involved so they can answer scope questions.
  6. Keep communication professional and written.

What happens after the appraisal award?

Once the award is signed, the carrier typically issues payment based on the award and the policy terms. In Texas, the Supreme Court's decisions in Barbara Technologies and Ortiz (2019) addressed how paying an award affects later prompt-payment and extra-contractual claims. Payment of an award does not automatically bar prompt-payment interest claims, but it generally limits most other extra-contractual claims. This is general information, not legal advice.

If the award is higher than what the carrier already paid, expect a supplemental payment for the difference. If you have a replacement cost policy, some of the award may be held as recoverable depreciation until repairs are complete. Our recoverable depreciation calculator can help you see how much may be released later and plan your repair schedule.

Common misconceptions about the timeline

  • "Appraisal always finishes quickly." Most do, but complex claims and umpire disputes take longer.
  • "The umpire decides everything." The umpire decides only items the appraisers cannot agree on.
  • "Appraisal always means a higher payment." Awards depend on the evidence; they do not always increase.
  • "Appraisal ends every dispute." It resolves amount; coverage disputes may continue separately.

Next steps: keep your appraisal moving

Warning signs that your timeline is drifting include an appraiser who will not return calls, months without an umpire, or repeated requests for the same documents. Address these early, in writing. An experienced appraiser keeps the process on schedule by preparing a strong estimate, submitting documentation early and communicating clearly with the other side.

faqs.q: How quickly must I name an appraiser after an appraisal demand?
faqs.a: Many Texas homeowners and commercial policies require each party to name an appraiser within 20 days after receiving the written demand, though wording varies. Check your policy's appraisal clause for the exact period. Selecting your appraiser before sending or responding to a demand helps you meet the deadline and keeps the process moving.

faqs.q: What happens if the appraisers cannot agree on an umpire?
faqs.a: If the two appraisers cannot agree on an umpire within the time set by the policy, either party can typically ask a court in the county where the property is located to appoint one. A court appointment usually adds weeks to the timeline, so appraisers often try hard to agree on a qualified, neutral umpire.

faqs.q: How long does the insurer have to pay after an appraisal award in Texas?
faqs.a: Timing depends on the policy and Texas law. Many policies set a payment period after the award, and Texas prompt-payment rules generally require payment within five business days after a claim is accepted. Interest and penalty questions after an award are legal issues, so consult a Texas attorney if payment is delayed.

faqs.q: Can I make repairs while the appraisal is ongoing?
faqs.a: You can usually make temporary repairs to prevent further damage, and you may need to under your policy. Before permanent repairs, make sure the damage is fully documented and both appraisers have had a chance to inspect. Removing evidence too early can weaken your position and slow down the process.

faqs.q: Does appraisal stop the Texas prompt payment clock?
faqs.a: Invoking appraisal does not erase the carrier's Chapter 542 obligations, and Texas Supreme Court decisions in 2019 held that paying an appraisal award does not automatically bar prompt-payment claims. How interest is calculated depends on the facts. This is a legal question best discussed with a Texas insurance attorney.
